sarf.text: For ṣarf, the Arabic letters fall into three groups: {{c1::the hamzah}}, {{c2::the weak letters, <bdi>حُرُوف العِلَّة</bdi>}} and {{c3::the sound letters, <bdi>حُرُوف صَحِيحَة</bdi> — all the rest}}
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07
IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: a regular, “sound” verb — no hamzah, no doubled letter and no weak letter among its roots
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.front: How do some grammarians use <bdi>صَحِيح</bdi> and <bdi>سَالِم</bdi> differently from the class?
sarf.back: For them <bdi>صَحِيح</bdi> is any verb that isn't <bdi>مُعْتَلّ</bdi>, and <bdi>سَالِم</bdi> is the sub-type that matches the class's <bdi>صَحِيح</bdi>
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.text: The irregular verbs are of three kinds: {{c1::<bdi>مَهْمُوز</bdi>}}, {{c2::<bdi>مُضَاعَف</bdi>}} and {{c3::<bdi>مُعْتَلّ</bdi>}}
sarf.extra: With a hamzah; with a doubled letter; with a weak letter.
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: a verb with a hamzah among its root letters, such as <bdi>أَكَلَ</bdi>
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.back: By which root letter is the hamzah: the fāʾ, as in <bdi>أَكَلَ</bdi>; the ʿayn, as in <bdi>سَأَلَ</bdi>; or the lām, as in <bdi>قَرَأَ</bdi>
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: a doubled verb: its second and third root letters are the same, such as <bdi>مَدَّ</bdi>
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: a weak verb: one with a weak letter among its roots
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.text: The kinds of <bdi>مُعْتَلّ</bdi>: {{c1::<bdi>مِثَال</bdi>}}, {{c2::<bdi>أَجْوَف</bdi>}}, {{c3::<bdi>نَاقِص</bdi>}}, {{c4::<bdi>لَفِيف مَقْرُون</bdi>}} and {{c5::<bdi>لَفِيف مَفْرُوق</bdi>}}
sarf.extra: The weak letter is first, second or third; then two weak letters, side by side or apart.
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: an assimilated verb: its first root letter is weak, such as <bdi>وَعَدَ</bdi>
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: a hollow verb: its second root letter is weak, such as <bdi>قَالَ</bdi>
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: a defective verb: its third root letter is weak, such as <bdi>دَعَا</bdi>
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: a verb with two weak letters side by side: the ʿayn and the lām, such as <bdi>طَوَى</bdi>
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: a verb with two weak letters apart: the fāʾ and the lām, such as <bdi>وَقَى</bdi>
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.front: <bdi>نَاقِص</bdi> means one thing of a verb in ṣarf and another in naḥw. What are they?
sarf.back: In ṣarf, a verb whose third root letter is weak, like <bdi>دَعَا</bdi>. In naḥw, an incomplete verb — <bdi>كَانَ</bdi> and her sisters — which needs a khabar.
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.front: Which two changes can apply to the hamzah of a <bdi>مَهْمُوز</bdi> verb?
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: lightening the hamzah: changing it to <bdi>ا</bdi>, <bdi>و</bdi> or <bdi>ي</bdi> to match the vowel before it
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.front: When must a hamzah be lightened, and when is it optional?
sarf.back: It must be when two hamzahs meet and the second is sākin: <bdi>أَأْمَنَ</bdi> becomes <bdi>آمَنَ</bdi>. A single sākin hamzah may be: <bdi>رَأْس</bdi> can be read <bdi>رَاس</bdi>.
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.meaning: dropping a letter from a word
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.front: In the amr of which four verbs is the hamzah most often dropped?
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.text: The amr of <bdi>أَكَلَ</bdi> is {{c1::<bdi>كُلْ</bdi>}}; of <bdi>أَخَذَ</bdi>, {{c2::<bdi>خُذْ</bdi>}}; of <bdi>أَمَرَ</bdi>, {{c3::<bdi>مُرْ</bdi>}}; of <bdi>سَأَلَ</bdi>, {{c4::<bdi>سَلْ</bdi>}}
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

sarf.front: For which of <bdi>كُلْ</bdi>, <bdi>خُذْ</bdi>, <bdi>مُرْ</bdi> and <bdi>سَلْ</bdi> does the hamzah stay dropped everywhere, and for which only at the start of speech?
sarf.back: Everywhere for <bdi>كُلْ</bdi> and <bdi>خُذْ</bdi>. For <bdi>مُرْ</bdi> and <bdi>سَلْ</bdi> only at the start: after <bdi>وَ</bdi> or <bdi>فَ</bdi> the hamzah usually returns, as in <bdi>وَأْمُرْ أَهْلَكَ بِالصَّلَاةِ</bdi> (20:132) and <bdi>وَاسْأَلِ القَرْيَةَ</bdi> (12:82).
sarf.source: IOK Arabic — Ṣarf: irregular verbs — class notes 2026-11-07

pyth.back: A way for programs to ask something questions programmatically. It isn't only for the web: programs that only ever run on one computer use APIs too.

pyth.front: Why would a program ask a web API rather than fetch a website's page?
pyth.back: The raw source of a modern, rich website runs to thousands and thousands of lines. An API answers the program's question directly, often as JSON.

pyth.front: In what format does a web API often respond, and how does Python read it?
pyth.back: JSON. The json module's json.loads() converts JSON text into Python data types: dictionaries, lists and so on.

pyth.front: Which module does URL (percent) encoding in Python, and what do you pass its urlencode?
pyth.back: urllib.parse. urlencode takes a list of tuples, one (name, value) pair per query parameter.
'q=lakers+clippers&maxResults=10' — each pair becomes name=value, joined by &. Here the space is encoded as +, which in a query string means the same as %20.

pyth.text: Accessing a web API, end to end: {{c1::build the URL, encoding the query parameters with urlencode}}; {{c2::make a Request and pass it to urlopen}}; {{c3::read the response and decode it as UTF-8}}; {{c4::convert the JSON text with json.loads}}; and {{c5::close the response, in a finally block}}

pyth.back: A list in which each element is a list, as in grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]

pyth.front:
What does this print?
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
print(grid[1][0])
pyth.back: 4 — grid[1] is the second inner list, and [0] is its first element

pyth.front: What does every object in a running Python program have, and what is guaranteed about it?
pyth.back: An ID, which id() returns. No two objects alive at the same time ever share one.

pyth.front:
What happens in memory here?
x = 5
x += 1
pyth.back:
The integer 5 isn't changed. x is re-attached to a different object, 6, so id(x) changes.
Before
After x += 1

pyth.front: How does a list hold its items in memory?

pyth.front:
What does this print, and why?
a = [1, 2]
before = id(a)
a.append(3)
print(id(a) == before)
pyth.back:
True — appending changes the list in place. It's still the same object, so its ID doesn't change.
Before
After a.append(3)

pyth.front:
What does this print, and why?
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
pyth.back: [1, 2, 3] — b = a copies nothing. Both names point at the same list, so a change made through one shows through the other.

pyth.front:
What does this print, and why?
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b = [9]
print(a)
pyth.back: [1, 2] — assigning to b again re-attaches it to a new object. a still points at the first list, which nothing changed.

pyth.front:
What does this print, and why?
def add_zero(nums):
    nums.append(0)

scores = [7, 8]
add_zero(scores)
print(scores)
pyth.back: [7, 8, 0] — passing a list to a function doesn't copy it. nums is another name for the caller's list, so the function changed a variable outside itself.

pyth.front:
What does this print, and why?
def bump(n):
    n += 1

x = 5
bump(x)
print(x)
pyth.back: 5 — n += 1 re-attaches n to a new object, 6. Nothing changed the 5 that x points at.
